title: Needs vs. wants
explanation: A need is something you must pay for to live, study or work safely (bus fare to school, food, books). A want makes life nicer but can wait (new headphones, eating out). Cover needs first, then decide on wants.
example: Your bus pass is a need. A movie with friends is a want, even if it feels important today.

title: Making a budget
explanation: A budget is a plan that gives every rupee a job before you spend it. Add up your money, list needs, set aside savings, and only then decide what is left for wants. Spending can never exceed income.

title: Short-term goals
explanation: A clear goal has an amount and a deadline. Divide the amount by the months you have to find how much to save each month.
example: A ₹1,200 calculator in 2 months needs ₹600 saved each month.

title: The saving habit
explanation: Saving works best as a habit: set money aside first, as soon as you receive it, instead of saving whatever is left at the end of the month (usually nothing).
example: Put ₹300 aside on the day you get your stipend, then budget the rest.

title: Emergency fund
explanation: An emergency fund is money kept aside only for surprises like medicine, repairs or a lost income. It protects your goals and helps you avoid borrowing.
example: A cracked phone screen is paid from the emergency fund, so your course savings stay untouched.

title: Simple vs. compound interest
explanation: Simple interest is paid only on the money you put in. Compound interest is also paid on interest already earned, so growth speeds up over time.
example: ₹1,000 at 10%: simple gives ₹100 every year; compound gives ₹100, then ₹110, then ₹121...

title: Risk and return
explanation: Options that can grow more usually swing more and can lose money. No investment offers high returns with no risk. Anyone promising guaranteed high returns is a warning sign.
example: A fixed deposit grows slowly but steadily; a single company's share can rise or fall 40% in a year.

title: Compounding over time
explanation: When returns are reinvested they start earning returns too. The longer money stays invested, the bigger this snowball effect becomes, which is why starting early matters.
example: Saving ₹500 a month from age 18 grows far more by 40 than starting at 28 with the same amount.

title: Diversification
explanation: Diversification means not putting all your eggs in one basket. Spreading money across many companies and types of assets means one failure cannot wipe you out.
example: A basket of 50 companies is less risky than one company, even a famous one.

title: Time horizon
explanation: Your time horizon is how long until you need the money. Money needed soon should stay in steady options; only money you will not need for many years can ride out market falls.
example: Fees due next year belong in a deposit, not in shares.

title: OTP and PIN safety
explanation: An OTP or UPI PIN is like the key to your money. Banks, police, companies and customer-care never ask for it. Entering your PIN always sends money out; you never need it to receive money.
example: 'Enter PIN to receive ₹2,000 cashback' is always a scam.

title: Phishing and fake links
explanation: Phishing messages pretend to be a trusted organisation and push you to click a link or call a number. Check the sender and web address, and use the official app or website instead of links in messages.
example: deccanbank-kyc-update.co is not your bank's website.

title: Too-good-to-be-true offers
explanation: Lotteries you never entered, jobs paying thousands for liking videos, and free phones are bait. If you must pay a fee to receive a prize or job, it is a scam.
example: 'Pay ₹499 registration to start earning ₹3,000/day' is a fake job.

title: Protecting personal data
explanation: Aadhaar, PAN, photos, addresses and contacts can be misused to take loans in your name or to blackmail. Share them only with verified institutions for a clear reason.
example: A giveaway asking for your Aadhaar photo is collecting data for fraud.

title: Inflation
explanation: Inflation means prices rise over time, so the same rupees buy a little less each year. Money that earns nothing slowly loses buying power, which is why a goal can cost more by the time you get there.
example: A ₹250 pair of earphones costing 6% more next year needs ₹265 then, so cash kept under a mattress buys less.
